planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown rosettes in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; cobweb houseleek needs sharp drainage and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil.

directions: Plant offsets or container-grown rosettes in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; cobweb houseleek needs sharp drainage and rots in heavy or poorly drained soil. Small, tight rosettes of fleshy, pointed leaves are laced across the tips with fine, white, web-like filaments that give the impression of a spider's cobweb draped over each rosette, an unmistakable and much-loved trait among the many hens-and-chicks species and cultivars. Extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant, native to rocky alpine slopes across the mountains of Europe, it forms an expanding mat of tightly packed rosettes that multiply readily by offsets, making it a classic, easy-care choice for a rock garden, stone wall crevice, or trough planting. Water only occasionally once established, and separate offsets to propagate or fill in bare patches, since each individual rosette is monocarpic and dies after flowering, leaving surrounding offsets to continue the colony.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown rosettes in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Blood Tip develops its darkest red tips with bright light and cool weather.

directions: Plant offsets or container-grown rosettes in spring in lean, gravelly, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Blood Tip develops its darkest red tips with bright light and cool weather. Pale green rosettes are dramatically tipped in deep blood-red at each leaf point, a striking two-tone color combination that intensifies in cooler weather and bright light, forming a spreading mat of tightly packed rosettes typical of hens-and-chicks. Extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, it multiplies readily by offsets to form an expanding colony, making it a colorful, low-maintenance choice for a rock garden, green roof, or trough planting. Water only occasionally, and separate offsets to propagate or fill bare patches as individual rosettes flower once and die, leaving the surrounding colony to continue.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Tricolor stonecrop holds its variegation best in bright light and can revert to solid green in shade.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Tricolor stonecrop holds its variegation best in bright light and can revert to solid green in shade. Small, rounded leaves are variegated in green, cream, and pink in a subtle but distinctive three-color pattern, spreading along low, trailing stems to form a dense, colorful groundcover mat, with small starry pink flowers appearing in summer above the variegated foliage. Extremely tolerant of poor soil, drought, and heat once established, it is a popular, easy-care groundcover for a sunny border edge, rock garden, or green roof planting, spreading steadily to fill in bare ground. Water only occasionally, remove any solid-green reverted growth to maintain the variegation, and divide congested mats to propagate or control spread.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this Pacific Northwest native sedum tolerates cooler, moister conditions than many drought-adapted sedum species.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this Pacific Northwest native sedum tolerates cooler, moister conditions than many drought-adapted sedum species. Small, rounded, opposite-paired, jelly-bean-like leaves in bright green often blush red at the tips in bright light, forming a low, spreading mat on rocky outcrops and cliffs from the Cascades to coastal bluffs of the Pacific Northwest, topped with small star-shaped yellow flowers in summer. Adapted to a cooler, wetter climate than many popular garden sedums bred from Mediterranean or Mexican species, it is a good native groundcover choice for a Pacific Northwest rock garden or dry border where more heat-loving sedums may struggle with the cooler summers. Water occasionally, particularly during establishment, and divide congested mats to propagate or control spread.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Oregon stonecrop tolerates cooler, moister Pacific Northwest conditions better than many drought-adapted sedum species.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in lean, rocky, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Oregon stonecrop tolerates cooler, moister Pacific Northwest conditions better than many drought-adapted sedum species. Glossy, spoon-shaped, bright green leaves often flush bronze-red in bright light or dry conditions, forming a low, spreading mat on rocky outcrops, forest edges, and coastal bluffs from California to British Columbia, topped with bright yellow, star-shaped flower clusters in early summer. One of the more shade-tolerant native western sedums, it grows in both open rock gardens and the light shade of a coastal forest edge, making it a versatile native groundcover for a Pacific Northwest rock garden or dry woodland border. Water occasionally, particularly during establishment, and divide congested mats to propagate or control spread.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Fire Spinner ice plant needs sharp drainage and is more cold-hardy than many other ice plant species.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Fire Spinner ice plant needs sharp drainage and is more cold-hardy than many other ice plant species. Small, fleshy, needle-like leaves cover a low, spreading mat smothered from late spring through fall in vivid, glistening, daisy-like flowers with a bold two-tone pattern of orange-red centers fading to purple-pink tips, a striking bicolor bloom that catches and reflects light with the characteristic 'icy' sheen the genus is named for. A Plant Select-introduced hybrid recognized for exceptional cold hardiness compared to most Delosperma species, it thrives in a xeriscape border, rock garden, or hot, dry parking strip planting with minimal supplemental water once established. Water only occasionally, shear lightly after the first flush of bloom to encourage continued flowering, and divide congested mats to propagate or refresh an aging planting.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Rosy ice plant needs sharp drainage and full sun for its best flowering display.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Rosy ice plant needs sharp drainage and full sun for its best flowering display. Slender, cylindrical, gray-green leaves cover a mounding, semi-woody South African succulent that produces a dazzling flush of glistening, deep rose-pink, daisy-like flowers each spring, densely covering the plant in color for several weeks and giving the whole planting a shimmering, iridescent quality typical of the ice plant group. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in coastal and Mediterranean-climate gardens, tolerating salt spray, poor soil, and neglect while providing a reliable, showy spring flower display for a sunny bank, rock garden, or xeriscape border. Water only occasionally, shear lightly after flowering to keep the mound tidy and encourage denser growth, and propagate easily from stem cuttings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
